method: Direct retrieval of public scholarly/institutional sources into reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/source-recheck-orality/ (curl -L; no search-engine snippets used as confirmation). WebSearch returned provider quota 403 and the DuckDuckGo HTML endpoint served a bot challenge, so retrieval went through archive.org item metadata/download plus heorot.dk and bosworthtoller.com. entry_sha256_before re-verified against both the working tree and 'git show fe34faa:<path>' immediately before the erratum append. Short excerpts below are quoted from the retrieved copies (OCR spacing normalised where noted) and each is under 40 words.

audits.claim: Kenning example: "whale-road" = sea (OE hronrād, The Seafarer) — i.e. the form hronrād is attributed to the poem The Seafarer.
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved: full Old English Beowulf text + translation (1,240,593-byte HTML, local copy); supplementary dictionary entry text retrieved in full from bosworthtoller.com
audits.source_locator: Beowulf line 10 (HTML lines 201-202); Bosworth-Toller online s.v. 'hwæl-weg' (entry text in search result page)
audits.source_excerpt: ofer hronráde  hýran scolde  ||  hwæl-weg, es; m. ... Hweteð on [h]wælweg hreðer unwearnum, Seef. 63
audits.basis: Passage retrieved. The compound hronrād is carried by Beowulf line 10 in the retrieved edition; the retrieved Bosworth-Toller entry gives The Seafarer's corresponding sea-compound as hwælweg (cited to 'Seef. 63', i.e. The Seafarer line 63). The entry's pairing therefore attaches a Beowulf form to The Seafarer: a wrong-fit citation, while the gloss 'whale-road = sea' itself stands. Dated erratum appended to the entry.
audits.access_limit: No full Old English text edition of The Seafarer could be retrieved (Wikisource search for 'hwælweg' returned 0 hits; sacred-texts mirror returned HTTP 403; Excel/Augsburg mirrors 404). The Seafarer form rests on Bosworth-Toller's citation of the line, so 'hronrād does not occur in The Seafarer' is an inference from the dictionary's citation practice, not a checked full-text absence.

audits.claim: Ballad technique ... the catchphrase "leaping and lingering" describes this style (Gummere 1907, The Popular Ballad, 91).
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved: full text of the 1907 Houghton Mifflin edition (687,416-byte DjVu transcription of the University of Toronto scan, local copy)
audits.source_locator: printed book index, transcription line 14338; running text, transcription line 11096 ('leaping' discussion at lines 3583-3591, 4608-4613)
audits.source_excerpt: Leaping  and  lingering,  91,   117,  283.  ...  of  the  alternate  leaping  and  lingering,  familiar  in  the
audits.basis: PASSAGE RETRIEVED. The phrase is the book's own indexed term (index line gives pp. 91, 117, 283), and the running text uses it in the retrieved body; the entry's attribution of the catchphrase to Gummere 1907 with p. 91 is confirmed at that locator level.
audits.access_limit: The body occurrence at transcription line 11096 was not mapped to its printed page from the scan's page index; the p. 91 anchor rests on the book's own index entry, not on a page-image check of p. 91 itself.

audits.claim: The Exeter Book preserves ~90 Old English riddles, several about writing itself (the book-consuming moth/worm).
audits.entry_locator: §7 'Riddles: taxonomy exams under a license to play', line 91
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved: full text of Tupper's 1910 scholarly edition (1,282,106-byte DjVu transcription, local copy)
audits.source_locator: Introduction on the received numeration, transcription lines 4687-4692; book-dependent riddles discussed at lines 2206, 3979, 4005-4006 ('Bookmoth (No. 48)', "two 'Book' problems (27, 68)")
audits.source_excerpt: by drawing four riddles into two, gives us eighty-nine in all ... He is followed by Assmann, who thus swells the number to ninety-five. ... the food of the Bookmoth (No. 48)
audits.basis: PASSAGE RETRIEVED. The 1910 edition reports counts of 89 (Grein) and 95 (Assmann and others), so '~90' is a fair rounding of an edition-dependent count rather than a factual error; a riddle about the book-eating moth is present in the corpus (Tupper's No. 48, modern Riddle 47), and Tupper additionally compares two book-related riddles, supporting 'several about writing itself'.
audits.access_limit: Tupper's numeration differs from modern editions (his No. 48 vs modern 47); no modern critical edition or manuscript facsimile was retrieved to state an exact modern total.

audits.claim: Proverbs are jurisprudence before codes: ... the lawspeaker recited a third of the law each assembly from the Law Rock (Íslendingabók / Grágás tradition) — law as performable text. (Coupling test: language/poetry tied to a ritual institution and an era.)
audits.entry_locator: §6 'Proverbs: the culture's compressed hard drive', line 85
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved: full Grágás (Konungsbók) text of Finsen's 1852 edition (963,491-byte DjVu transcription, local copy); Íslendingabók Icelandic text retrieved separately (95,773-byte page, is.wikisource.org)
audits.source_locator: Grágás, Þingskapa þáttr, '19. misseris tal', printed p. 37 — running headers '36 GRÁGÍS' (line 1486) and '38 GRÁGÁS' (line 1558) bracket the passage; quoted clause at lines 1548-1553. Íslendingabók: lawspeaker recitation at Wikisource HTML lines 835 and 887.
audits.source_excerpt: Lög oll ... vera sogd ypp aþrimr sumrum. scal þa logsogy maþr af h^ndí bioþá lavgsogyna. ... oc sca\ at logb^rgi ... vpp segía    ||    hann keypti at Þorgeiri lögsögumanni, at hann skyldi upp segja
audits.basis: PASSAGE RETRIEVED. Grágás states that all the laws are to be spoken up over three summers ('sögð upp á þrimr sumrum'), i.e. one third at each annual summer assembly, and places recitation at the Law Rock in the same section ('at lögbergi ... upp segja'). The Íslendingabók passage retrieved shows the lawspeaker's 'upp segja' duty being traded/assigned, and ch. 10 of the same text records the first writing of the law ('lög ór skyldi skrifa á bók', Wikisource line 887) — the oral-recitation to written-code transition the entry couples. Verdict applies to the coupling claim as a tradition-level statement; see access limit for the OCR basis.
audits.access_limit: The 1852 scan is OCR-noisy (Fraktur-derived: 'sogd ypp' = sögð upp, 'logb^rgi' = lögbergi, 'sca\' = skal); normalised readings are given in brackets in the basis, and no English critical translation (e.g. Laws of Early Iceland) was retrieved. The p. 37 page anchor is inferred from the bracketing running headers, not from page images.

audits.claim: Avdo Medđedović's The Wedding of Smailagić Meho, 12,323 lines in one performance (§1); and §10 'the 12,323-line Meho figure is Lord's own count (Lord 1960)'.
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved: full text of the Internet Archive scan of Lord, The Singer of Tales (869,106-byte DjVu transcription, local copy)
audits.source_locator: transcription lines 6131-6132 (Avdo's assembly theme / song-book learning) and lines 7739-7741 (summary of the learning case)
audits.source_excerpt: his dictated version runs to over 12,000 lines ... This is the case of Avdo Mededovié and the twelve thousand-line dictated text of "The Wedding of Smailagić Meho" (Parry 6840).
audits.basis: PASSAGE RETRIEVED BUT DOES NOT CONFIRM THE CLAIM AS WORDED. The retrieved 1960 text supports the ~12,000-line magnitude but characterises the text as dictated ('dictated version', 'twelve thousand-line dictated text') and nowhere in the retrieved scan does the string '12,323' occur (searched). A dictated transcript taken down from singing is not described by the entry as 'one performance', and the attribution of the exact numeral to Lord 1960 is not supported by this edition. Dated erratum appended flagging the framing and keeping the exact figure to-verify.
audits.access_limit: The later print where 12,323 lines is normally given (Serbo-Croatian Heroic Songs, The Wedding of Smailagić Meho, Harvard UP) and the Harvard Milman Parry Collection catalogue page could not be retrieved: WebSearch was quota-blocked (HTTP 403), archive.org advancedsearch for 'Smailagic' returned unrelated records, and only the general collection page (no line count) was fetched. Exact figure provenance therefore remains unverified.

notes: No erratum was appended for ORALITY-02 or ORALITY-03 (both supported). Errata were appended only to the two demonstrably supported corrections (ORALITY-01 wrong-fit citation; ORALITY-05 framing), preserving all prior corpus bytes. Oral/literary 'Great Divide' claims were not endorsed: this recheck extracted no support for strong-version cognitive-divide positions, and no such statement in the entry was treated as verified here. Retrieval artefacts remain in reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/source-recheck-orality/ for parent spot-checks.
